01

The short version

Say it this way

Future of Gas is an Illinois Commerce Commission case built around one question. How should Illinois think about the gas system as the state moves toward its clean energy goals? It does not write rules. It produces a report by December 31 that informs the Commission and the legislature. We are in the last working phase now, and three points matter. The study is a thought exercise, not a plan. The hybrid scenarios hold up well in it. And it shares its models with the electric resource plan.

What Future of Gas is

Future of Gas, usually shortened to FOG, is an Illinois Commerce Commission proceeding (Docket 24-0158) that asks one big question. How should Illinois think about the natural gas system as the state pursues its clean energy goals? The ICC opened it in March 2024, and it grew out of the November 2023 gas rate case orders for Illinois utilities.

FOG does not make rules. It gathers facts, hears from many groups, and produces a final report due December 31, 2026. That report informs the Commission and the General Assembly. Any real change in law or rates would come later, through legislation or separate ICC cases.

Where things stand on October 2, 2026

  • The proceeding is in Phase 2C, the last working phase. Groups have submitted policy proposals, and next come workshops, staff recommendations and the final report.
  • The E3 Decarbonization Pathways Study compares five ways Illinois could get gas sector emissions to net zero by 2050. A final version is expected in early October.
  • Amended proposals are due to the facilitator on October 16 under the ICC template. Workshops on them are planned for October 26 and 27.
  • ICC staff draft recommendations come at a workshop on November 9.
  • The final FOG report is due December 31, 2026.

Three things to remember

  1. The study is a thought exercise, not a plan. E3 worked backward from net zero in 2050, and the study says itself that none of the scenarios is an optimal pathway.
  2. The hybrid scenarios look strong in the study. Hybrid Electrification cuts direct emissions by about 87 percent, close to the 89 percent for High Electrification, while loading the electric grid far less.
  3. The study and the electric Integrated Resource Plan are linked. They use the same E3 models, and the study's Hybrid Electrification case lines up with an electrification case in the IRP.
02

Plain-language glossary

Say it this way

If a term trips you up, here is the short version. A back-cast starts at the goal and works backward. A heat pump moves heat instead of making it. A hybrid pairs a heat pump with a gas furnace for the coldest days. Net zero means cutting emissions as far as possible and balancing the rest. Peak demand is the highest hour of use, and winter heating could push the electric peak up sharply.

The words that come up most, with what each means and why it matters here.

Proceeding and policy terms

TermWhat it meansWhy it matters here
ICCThe Illinois Commerce Commission. It regulates utility rates and service in Illinois.It runs FOG and decides utility rate cases.
FOGFuture of Gas. The ICC proceeding on the long-term role of gas utilities.Everything on this page ties back to it.
DocketThe official case file for a proceeding, with a number such as 24-0158.Comments and filings go on the docket.
FacilitatorCelia Johnson, who runs the workshops and collects proposals and comments.Amended proposals go to her.
CEJAThe Climate and Equitable Jobs Act. State law that sets clean energy goals, including a move to 100 percent clean power.It frames why FOG exists.
Net zeroEmissions cut as far as possible, with the small remainder balanced by removing carbon or avoiding methane.The study works backward from net zero by 2050.
80x50A slower goal of an 80 percent cut by 2050.E3 ran it as a side test.
Phase 2CThe current phase, with workshops on policy proposals and review of the E3 study.This is where the proposals are debated.
Legislative or regulatory proposalA written idea for a new law or ICC rule, submitted by a stakeholder.Ameren Illinois filed six.

Energy and modeling terms

TermWhat it meansWhy it matters here
Back-castStart at the end goal and work backward to see what must happen each year. A forecast does the opposite.It is why the study is not a prediction.
ScenarioOne consistent story of how the system might change.E3 built five, plus a baseline.
BAUBusiness as usual. The baseline with no new decarbonization push beyond current law.The comparison point for every result.
Hybrid heatingA heat pump handles most of the year and a gas furnace takes over on the coldest days.The heart of the Hybrid scenarios.
Heat pumpAn electric device that moves heat rather than making it. Very efficient in mild weather.The study assumes a big jump in heat pump sales.
Ground-source (geothermal) heat pumpA heat pump that draws heat from the ground, which stays near a steady temperature.It drives the High Geothermal scenario.
Thermal energy networkShared underground piping that moves heat between buildings, with heat pumps at each site.Ameren Illinois proposal G.1.
RNGRenewable natural gas. Pipeline-quality gas made from waste such as landfills and farms.Proposal A.1. Supply and price are central questions.
SNGSynthetic natural gas, made from hydrogen and captured carbon.Expensive and early stage.
TBtuTrillion British thermal units. A way to count energy.The study shows about 200 TBtu of gas use left in 2050 even in the lowest gas case.
CCSCarbon capture and storage. Catching carbon dioxide and burying it.Used in every scenario to reach net zero.
TRLTechnology readiness level. A 1 to 9 scale of how proven a technology is.Helps judge how realistic each scenario is.
Peak demand and coincident peakPeak demand is the highest use in a period. Coincident peak is the total when everyone's use peaks together.Winter heating could push the electric peak up sharply.
Reliability needThe generating capacity required to meet peak demand with a safety cushion on top.A key electric grid measure in the results.
ELCCEffective load carrying capability. How much a resource can be counted on at peak time.Wind and solar count for less at winter peak than a gas plant.
PLEXOS and RECAPThe computer models E3 uses for system operations and for reliability.The same models support the IRP.
Managed vs unmanaged transitionManaged means the gas system shrinks on purpose, with planning. Unmanaged means customers leave on their own and the system shrinks unevenly.The study shows costs landing on the customers who remain.
NPANon-pipeline alternative. Spending on something other than a new gas pipe, such as electrification, to meet the same need.Behind the zonal idea.
LEALine extension allowance. What a gas utility pays toward connecting a new customer to the main.A lever regulators can use on gas system growth.

Utility planning terms

TermWhat it meansWhy it matters here
IRPIntegrated Resource Plan. A long-range plan for how the electric system will meet demand.It reuses E3 models, so it overlaps with FOG.
Resource adequacyHaving enough power supply to keep the lights on at the worst moments.A January 2026 study showed risk in MISO and PJM during 2028 to 2031.
Mitigation planThe plan to fix those resource adequacy risks.Its timing does not line up with FOG.
MISO and PJMThe two regional grid operators that cover Illinois. MISO serves most of the Ameren Illinois area. PJM serves ComEd.They shape the reliability numbers.
Revenue balancing adjustmentA rate tool that ties collected revenue to the approved amount instead of to how much gas is sold.Proposal F.6.
Zonal electrificationElectrifying a defined zone and phasing out its gas service, one area at a time.Proposal C.1.
03

The process so far

Say it this way

This started with the 2023 gas rate cases. The ICC opened Future of Gas in March 2024 and has run it in phases, from collecting topics, to digging into pathways, to splitting into pilots and pathways groups, to today's phase where groups put forward policy proposals. Next come amended proposals on October 16, workshops on October 26 and 27, staff recommendations on November 9, and the final report on December 31.

The story in order. Each phase built on the one before it.

Where it started

In late 2023 the ICC issued final orders in the gas rate cases for Illinois utilities. Concerns about long-term gas investment and clean energy goals led the Commission to open a broader proceeding. Its initiating order came in March 2024, under Docket 24-0158.

Phase by phase

PhaseWhat happenedWhy it mattered
Phase 1Topic gathering. Stakeholders put decarbonization ideas on the table.It set the list of questions for the rest of the proceeding.
Phase 2AA deeper technical look at decarbonization pathways.It added detail on what the options would take.
Phase 2BWorking groups on pilots and on pathways.The pathways group led to the E3 study. The pilots work led to a separate docket on pilot authority.
Phase 2CWorkshops on legislative and regulatory proposals, stakeholder feedback, and review of the E3 results.Where Ameren Illinois' six proposals are being debated.
Final reportA report to the Commission and the General Assembly, due December 31, 2026.It ends the proceeding but does not set rules.

Phase 2C step by step

  1. June 2026. The ICC published a draft Phase 2C report summarizing the initial proposals.
  2. July 2026. Stakeholders sent feedback on those proposals.
  3. September 24. E3 presented the Pathways Study results. An updated deck followed on October 1.
  4. October 16. Amended proposals are due to the facilitator, using the ICC template.
  5. October 26 and 27. Workshops where submitters can present amended proposals, if needed.
  6. November 9. ICC staff present draft recommendations.
  7. Late November. A Phase 2 summary report goes out for comment.
  8. December 31. The final FOG report is due.
Who is who

ICC staff guide the process and will make draft recommendations. E3 is the consulting firm that built the Pathways Study. Celia Johnson is the independent facilitator. Stakeholders include utilities, consumer and environmental groups, the RNG Coalition and others.

04

The E3 Pathways Study, explained

Say it this way

E3 built a back-cast to net zero by 2050 with five scenarios. It was never meant to pick a winner. What stands out is that Hybrid Electrification gets close to the emissions cut of full electrification, 87 percent against 89, with far less strain on the electric grid. Peak demand grows 75 percent in the hybrid case and 130 percent in High Electrification. Reviewers will still ask about how fast heat pumps can be adopted, whether the alternative fuel supply is real, and who would run carbon capture.

What the study is trying to do

The ICC asked E3 to build a shared set of facts about how Illinois could cut gas sector emissions. The goal is a common analytical base that everyone can argue from, not a recommended plan. E3 states that none of its scenarios is an optimal pathway.

How a back-cast works

Most forecasts start today and project forward. A back-cast fixes the end point first, then asks what must be true in each earlier year to land there. The study fixes net zero by 2050 and a 35 percent cut by 2035, and it also runs a slower 80 percent by 2050 side case.

The five scenarios plus the baseline

ScenarioPlain-language ideaWhat it leans on
BAUBusiness as usual. The baseline.Current policy only.
High ElectrificationMove almost all buildings to electric heat.Heat pumps in nearly every home, a large grid buildout, and a very small gas system.
High GeothermalElectrify with a big role for ground-source heat pumps.Ground-source systems cut winter peak load. Cost and installation pace are open questions.
Hybrid ElectrificationHeat pumps do most of the work, with gas furnaces for the coldest days.A hybrid system in most homes, plus a smaller amount of low-carbon gas.
Hybrid GasA hybrid with a larger role for gas.More low-carbon gas, where supply and price questions grow.
Continued Gas UseKeep the gas system largely as is and decarbonize the fuel.A very large amount of alternative fuel, plus carbon capture.

What the study measured

E3 judged each scenario on 18 evaluation measures in 7 groups, including system cost, customer affordability, grid reliability, air quality, technology readiness, jobs and workforce. Darker boxes below mean more risk or more tradeoff.

Results worth knowing

Emissions, and what carries the last mile

High Electrification and High Geothermal cut direct emissions by 89 percent. Hybrid Electrification reaches 87 percent. Hybrid Gas and Continued Gas Use reach 78 percent. Every scenario still needs captured carbon to reach net zero, and the two gas-heavy cases lean on it most.

What happens to the gas system

Gas use falls by 79 to 82 percent in the three electrification scenarios and by 42 to 56 percent in the two gas-heavy cases. Even so, about 200 TBtu of gas use remains in 2050 in the lowest gas case, because no pathway fully removes commercial, industrial and hydrogen demand. In the study, the cost of the gas system is spread over the customers who remain, so the bill for those who stay climbs as others leave.

Check before quoting

The text on slide 28 describes rate increases of roughly 4 times and 25 times, and the chart labels on the same slide do not match those multiples. The deck shows Nicor Gas rates and does not show gas results for Ameren Illinois. Confirm both points with the final report.

What happens to the electric grid

Peak demand grows by 130 percent in High Electrification across ComEd and Ameren combined, and by 75 percent in Hybrid Electrification. In Ameren territory, E3's chart shows a total reliability need of nearly 29 GW for High Electrification against about 21 GW for Hybrid Electrification (slide 81).

Costs and who benefits

When health and climate benefits are counted, Hybrid Electrification has the largest net societal benefit, about $150 billion over 2025 to 2050. High Electrification is the smallest, and its range crosses zero.

What it means for a customer in Ameren territory

For a single-family home in Ameren territory, the average monthly energy bill today is about $238 with a standard gas furnace. Electrifying raises the near-term bill by 4 to 14 percent, except with a ground-source heat pump, which comes in lower.

How a hybrid system works

In a hybrid home, a heat pump supplies heat for most of the year because it is very efficient in mild weather. When it gets cold, a gas furnace takes over. E3 models a switchover near 20 degrees Fahrenheit. The furnace runs fewer hours, but those hours are the coldest ones and they decide the winter peak. That is why a hybrid can cut emissions without forcing the electric grid to serve the whole winter peak.

Questions reviewers are likely to raise

TopicWhy it draws questions
Customer costs and ratesThe study spreads the gas system cost over a shrinking group of customers, which makes outcomes look less fair for gas customers.
Heat pump adoptionThe study assumes annual heat pump sales of about 4 to 4.5 times today's level.
Alternative fuelsThe study assumes a very large volume of alternative fuels by 2050 at assumed prices. Reviewers will ask about feedstock and price evidence.
Carbon captureUsed in every scenario, and the study narrative says little about who would build, permit and run it.
Technology mixed with fuelSome charts pair equipment with expensive alternative fuels, so equipment cost and fuel cost are hard to separate.
EV and data center loadHigh growth at non-peak times may hold down apparent residential rate impacts.
05

How the proceedings connect

Say it this way

Future of Gas is one of several efforts that overlap. The electric resource plan uses the same E3 models. The resource adequacy work covers reliability risk in MISO and PJM. The pilot docket sets rules for pilots, and the zonal study feeds a future rate case. The timelines do not line up, so the way one is described can shape how another is read.

FOG does not sit alone. Several other efforts feed it or draw from it, and their schedules do not line up.

The IRP overlap

Both the IRP and the E3 study use E3 and the same electric models. The study's BAU case matches the IRP Base Case, and the study's Hybrid Electrification case lines up with the IRP's electrification case. Reviewers should read the two side by side, since the choice of scenario drives how much new capacity the IRP has to plan for.

The other pieces

ItemStatusWhy it matters to Ameren Illinois
Pilot process docketA proposed order addresses ICC authority over pilots, cost recovery and customer data sharing. Customer data sharing requires consent.It sets the rules for any hybrid or electrification pilot.
Zonal electrification studyA study of representative sites that is meant to feed a future gas rate case.It supports the Zonal Electrification Tariff proposal.
IRPFiling expected in mid November.Draws on the same E3 models.
Resource adequacy study and mitigation planA January 2026 study shows risk in MISO and PJM during 2028 to 2031. A mitigation plan follows.Ties to reliability and capacity discussions.
Multi-Year Grid Plan and future rate casesStudy outputs are meant to inform them.This is where proposals could turn into rates.
06

The Ameren Illinois lens

Say it this way

Ameren Illinois serves more than 800,000 gas customers and 1.2 million electric customers across about three quarters of the state, mostly small cities, towns and farmland. Our position is a hybrid pathway that keeps customer choice and resilience, gives us options, and invests in leak detection. We filed six proposals, and the study's hybrid results support several of them.

Reader note

This page is a personal learning guide built from public sources. It is not an official statement of Ameren Illinois positions. Check any proposal detail against the filed documents on the ICC Future of Gas page.

Ameren Illinois at a glance

ItemFigureWhy it helps you read the study
CustomersAbout 1.2 million electric and more than 800,000 natural gas customersA dual-fuel utility, so electrification moves customers from one of its systems to the other.
TerritoryAbout 43,700 square miles, roughly three quarters of Illinois, 89 counties and about 1,200 communitiesMostly small cities, towns and farmland, not a dense big-city system.
Gas systemAbout 18,700 miles of gas mains and 12 underground storage fields holding about 24 billion cubic feetStorage and mains stand behind a winter peak.
Electric systemAbout 4,600 miles of transmission lines and 46,000 miles of distribution linesHeat pumps at scale would test these lines on cold mornings.
Planning gridMISO serves most of the areaE3 shows Ameren territory separately from ComEd in several charts.

Source is the Ameren Illinois fact sheet. Figures change, so check the current sheet.

The stated position

Ameren Illinois has described its view as a hybrid pathway that keeps customer choice and resilience, provides optionality, and invests in leak detection. Several E3 results fit that view, especially the Hybrid Electrification scenario.

The six proposals

ProposalWhat it asks for, in plain wordsWhere the study helps or raises questions
RNG Interconnection Incentive (A.1)Turn the seven-year revenue test into an upfront incentive for RNG producers, framed as rate neutral.The study assumes a very large volume of alternative fuel, so supply and price are the main questions.
Zonal Electrification Tariff (C.1)Create a proceeding to resolve contested issues from the zonal electrification study.The zonal study feeds this.
Hybrid Heat Pump Program (C.2)Incentives and rebates for pairing heat pumps with gas furnaces to reduce gas throughput while protecting winter reliability.The Hybrid scenarios are the strongest support.
Emissions Reduction Act (D.1)A voluntary capital plan for utility decarbonization investments, as an alternative to a mandatory clean heat standard.The deck does not test this approach directly.

Thermal Energy Networks Act (G.1)Allow utility ownership and operation of thermal energy network assets.High Geothermal results show networks can ease peak load.
07

The proposals explained for a first-time reader

Say it this way

Think of the six proposals as six different tools. Hybrids and thermal networks change the equipment. The zonal tariff sets up a process for retiring old pipe. RNG changes the fuel in the pipe. The revenue balancing adjustment changes how the utility is paid. And the Emissions Reduction Act is a voluntary investment plan.

Each proposal answers the same questions. What is it, where has it been used, who owns what, what does it cost, how long does it take, where would it fit, and what are the pros and cons. Cost figures come from published sources and many come from other states or vendor guides, so they show scale and not a quote for any Ameren Illinois customer.

How to read the cost numbers

Numbers come from a named report, a web source or the E3 deck. Where simple arithmetic was done, it is marked as an illustration. No number here is an Ameren Illinois estimate. Proposal level costs are in the filed proposals on the ICC site.

C.2

Hybrid Heat Pump Program

Say it this way

A hybrid system keeps the gas furnace and adds a heat pump. The heat pump does most of the year, and the furnace takes over on the coldest days. That helps the electric grid because the furnace covers the winter peak. The program would help pay for the heat pump. The open questions are who pays the incentive and whether the bill savings show up for customers.

In one sentence. A utility rebate program that helps homeowners add an electric heat pump to a home that keeps its gas furnace, so the heat pump runs most of the year and the furnace covers the coldest days.

Where it is used

Dual-fuel systems are sold widely in the United States where winters are cold enough to need a backup. E3 models a switchover near 20 degrees Fahrenheit. RMI analyzed hybrid systems for Illinois.

Who owns what

The homeowner owns the equipment and a contractor installs it. The utility funds an incentive and, as a dual-fuel company, serves the home with both gas and electricity.

Typical cost
  • Published installed cost estimates for dual-fuel systems range from roughly $7,000 up to $20,000 or more, depending on home size, ductwork and equipment (industry buying guides).
  • RMI's Illinois analysis says a hybrid part-load system costs about $1,000 to $2,000 more than replacing an air conditioner alone. A full-load cold climate heat pump costs about $2,000 to $8,000 more than replacing a furnace and air conditioner.
  • RMI reports Illinois utilities now pay about $500 to $2,000 per air-source heat pump, and suggests $2,000 for hybrid systems and $8,000 for full-load systems.
  • Equipment life is about 15 to 20 years.
Bill effect
  • In the E3 appendix, a single-family home in Ameren territory has an average bill of about $251 per month with a hybrid and gas appliances, against about $238 with a standard gas furnace today.
  • RMI estimated hybrid customers of Nicor Gas would save only about $20 per year, partly because gas fixed charges stay high.
Time to build

An install takes a day or two. Scale is limited by contractor capacity and the 15 to 20 year equipment cycle. E3 assumes heat pump sales of 4 to 4.5 times today's level, which is a fast ramp.

Urban or rural fit

Best in single-family homes with central air conditioning and ductwork in gas-served towns and cities such as Peoria, Springfield, Champaign-Urbana and Decatur. RMI says about 90 percent of Illinois homes have central air, so the air conditioner replacement is a natural moment to offer a hybrid.

Investment scale

Illustration only. A $2,000 incentive for 50,000 homes would be a $100 million pool. Ameren Illinois has more than 800,000 gas customers, so 50,000 homes is about 6 percent.

Pros
  • Cuts winter electric peak far below full electrification. E3 shows peak growth of 75 percent for Hybrid Electrification against 130 percent for High Electrification.
  • Keeps a gas furnace as backup, which supports resilience.
  • Lower upfront cost than going all-electric.
  • Reduces gas use and emissions.
Cons
  • The homeowner maintains two systems.
  • Bill savings are small or negative today.
  • Incentives are paid by ratepayers.
  • Needs controls and the right electric rate to work well.
Questions to ask

Who pays the incentive, gas or electric customers? Which electric rate would hybrid customers get? What do pilots show about real switchover behavior?

G.1

Thermal Energy Networks

Say it this way

A thermal energy network is a shared loop of water underground. Each building has a heat pump that pulls heat from the loop in winter and puts heat back in summer. The first utility network in the country, in Framingham, took about four years from approval to operation and serves about 135 customers. It works best in dense areas, and the cost per customer is still high at pilot scale.

In one sentence. Instead of piping gas to each building, a utility builds a shared underground loop of water that stays near ground temperature, and each building uses a heat pump to take heat from the loop in winter or return it in summer.

Where it is used
  • Eversource in Framingham, Massachusetts, the first utility-run network in the United States. It serves about 135 customers, including 24 single-family homes, 100 city housing apartments, some public buildings and five commercial buildings.
  • National Grid in Lowell, Massachusetts, where construction began in April 2023.
  • New York passed a 2022 law, and utilities filed 13 pilot proposals in December 2023, including Con Edison projects at Rockefeller Center and in Chelsea.
  • Campus and community systems already run at Colorado Mesa University, Weber State University and Whisper Valley in Texas.
Who owns what

There are three models. In the utility-owned model a gas or electric utility builds, owns and operates the loop and bills customers. In the community or developer model a campus or private developer runs it. In the non-utility model, grants fund studies and pilots. Each building owns or leases its heat pump. Ameren Illinois' proposal asks that utilities be allowed to own and operate, without making that exclusive.

Typical cost
  • Framingham was estimated at about $14 million for about 135 customers. That is roughly $100,000 per customer, but it is arithmetic on a first-of-a-kind pilot and not a forecast.
  • Boreholes are typically 100 to 600 feet deep.
  • Illinois has set aside up to $20 million for neighborhood-scale networks under the CRGA, and the Illinois Climate Bank has up to $15 million in geothermal grants aimed at about 1,100 households.
Time to build

Framingham was approved in 2020, broke ground in June 2023 and was commissioned in June 2024. That is about four years from approval to operation, followed by a two-season monitoring period.

Urban or rural fit

Works best where buildings sit close together, such as downtown blocks, campuses, apartment clusters and new subdivisions, and where old gas pipes are due for replacement. Low-density rural areas are a poor fit because the loop is long and customers are few.

Illinois status

The CRGA (SB 25) passed in the October 2025 veto session and created a TEN pilot program run by the ICC and the Illinois Finance Authority. A separate bill, HB 3609, would have let investor-owned gas and dual-fuel utilities build up to three projects. It cleared committee in April 2025 but did not get a floor vote. In August 2025 ICC staff picked three TEN pilot ideas from the FOG process, in Elmhurst, at Loyola University Chicago and in the City of Chicago.

Pros
  • Very efficient. DOE puts the energy cut at about 44 percent for ground-source versus air-source heat pumps.
  • Lowers winter peak electric demand compared with air-source heat pumps.
  • Uses utility skills and gas workforce.
  • One system heats and cools.
  • Can use pipe replacement dollars.
Cons
  • High cost per customer at pilot scale.
  • Needs dense customer clusters.
  • Needs rate rules for a new kind of service.
  • Drilling and construction take years.
  • Debate over whether utilities should own the loops.
Questions to ask

Would a pilot run under the proposal or under the CRGA program? How would costs be recovered if customers join slowly? How does it affect the gas pipe replacement plan?

C.1

Zonal Electrification Tariff

Say it this way

Zonal electrification means choosing an area, helping everyone in it move to electric heat, and retiring the old gas pipe instead of replacing it. The proposal asks the ICC to open a proceeding to settle the hard questions, like who pays and whether it is voluntary. Our zonal study should give us real numbers.

In one sentence. Pick a defined zone, offer every customer in it a move to electric heat, and retire the gas main serving the zone, so the utility avoids replacing an old pipe. The tariff is the set of rate rules that make that possible. The proposal asks the ICC to open a proceeding to settle the contested issues that come out of the zonal study.

Where it is used
  • This is the idea behind non-pipeline alternatives, where a utility meets a need with something other than a new pipe. From general knowledge that was not re-checked here, California authorized zonal electrification pilots by law in 2024 and New York regulators have looked at non-pipeline options. Verify before citing.
  • Ameren Illinois' own zonal study looks at representative sites and is meant to feed a future gas rate case.
Who owns what

Customers own their new equipment. The utility owns the electric upgrades and either retires or keeps the gas main. Who pays for customers' equipment, and whether participation is voluntary, are the contested questions.

Typical cost

No sourced figure fits Ameren territory yet, and the study is meant to produce one. For scale, Peoples Gas asked for a $402 million rate increase largely to fund aging pipe replacement, which shows how large the avoided cost can be.

Time to build

Several years. The zone must be chosen, customers must sign up, the electric system may need upgrades, and then the main can be retired.

Urban or rural fit

Strongest where old mains are costly to replace and homes are close together. In rural zones, long mains serve few customers, which also makes retirement attractive, but the electric system may be thin there.

Pros
  • Avoids replacing costly mains.
  • Cuts gas system cost that would otherwise fall on remaining customers.
  • Targets the places where it saves the most.
  • Creates a clear process instead of case by case fights.
Cons
  • Needs nearly everyone in the zone to switch, which raises consent and fairness questions.
  • Needs electric capacity.
  • Customers lose gas choice.
  • Equity concerns if some customers cannot afford the change.
Questions to ask

Is participation voluntary? Who pays for customers' equipment? How does it tie to the Multi-Year Grid Plan so electric upgrades come first?

A.1

RNG Interconnection Incentive

Say it this way

Renewable natural gas is gas made from landfills, farms and wastewater that goes into the same pipes. Today a producer's connection depends on a seven year revenue test, and the proposal turns that into an upfront incentive. The big questions are how much real supply exists in our region and what it costs. The study puts it near $46 per MMBtu in 2050, against about $2.80 for gas today.

In one sentence. Renewable natural gas is pipeline-quality gas made from waste. The proposal turns the utility's seven-year revenue test for connecting a producer into an upfront incentive, framed as rate neutral, so more projects can connect.

Where it is used

California has the most developed program. Its Biomethane Monetary Incentive Program provided $80 million, then ran out of money with a waitlist of viable projects, according to a filing in that state. California regulators also reported interconnection costs there are two to three times higher than in other states.

Who owns what

The producer, such as a landfill, dairy or wastewater plant, owns the capture and cleanup equipment and usually pays upfront. The utility owns its pipeline and the interconnection point. Under the proposal the utility would pay an incentive toward the interconnection instead of testing whether seven years of revenue repay the cost.

Typical cost
  • Interconnection can be a large share of a small project's budget. The California filing noted some agreements carry contingencies up to 100 percent above projected cost.
  • RNG is expensive. The E3 deck puts biomethane at about $46 per MMBtu in 2050, while gas costs about $2.80 today.
Time to build

The gas flows once the producer's project is built and connected. Waste-to-gas projects commonly take several years from planning to operation. That is a general industry pattern and not a sourced figure.

Urban or rural fit

Mostly rural and edge of town, near farms, landfills and wastewater plants. Central and southern Illinois is heavily agricultural, which suggests potential. The study assumes a very large national-scale volume, so a regional supply assessment is a fair question to ask.

Pros
  • Uses the pipes and furnaces customers already have.
  • Captures methane that would otherwise escape.
  • Can bring income to farms and landfills.
  • Does not require customers to change equipment.
Cons
  • Limited supply and high price.
  • Every ratepayer would fund an incentive that benefits producers.
  • Emissions savings depend on how the gas is counted.
  • The volume assumed in the study is very large compared with known supply.
Questions to ask

How large is the real RNG supply in central and southern Illinois? Would the incentive have a cap? How is rate neutral measured?

F.6

Gas Revenue Balancing Adjustment

Say it this way

A revenue balancing adjustment lets the utility collect the revenue the ICC approved, no more and no less. If sales fall, charges adjust. That removes any reason to sell more gas, but it also means each unit costs more if sales keep falling, which is why people want guardrails.

In one sentence. A rate tool that lets the utility collect the revenue the ICC approved, not more and not less, by adjusting charges up or down to make up for weather and falling sales. It is sometimes called revenue decoupling because earnings no longer depend on how much gas is sold.

Where it is used
  • A U.S. Department of Energy summary listed 18 states with approved gas decoupling as of January 2010, including Illinois, Colorado, California, Massachusetts, New York and Wisconsin.
  • The Illinois Supreme Court upheld a volume balancing adjustment rider for a gas utility. The court said the ICC's decision deserved deference and did not break rules against retroactive or single-issue ratemaking.
  • The proposal would move from the current volume-based balancing to a construct like the electric side.
Who owns what

There are no physical assets. The ICC approves the revenue amount, the utility files the true-up, and customers pay a surcharge or get a credit.

Typical cost

It does not add revenue, because it collects the approved amount. It moves who bears the risk. In a mild year or when use falls, customers pay a surcharge. In a cold year, they get a credit.

Time to build

It needs ICC approval, usually in a rate case, then a yearly filing and review.

Urban or rural fit

It applies to all gas customers in a rate class, so there is no urban or rural split. How impacts fall across customer classes is a key question.

Pros
  • Removes the utility's incentive to sell more gas, which supports efficiency and hybrid programs.
  • Stabilizes revenue and sometimes bills.
  • Cuts the need for frequent rate cases.
Cons
  • When fewer customers or units remain, each unit costs more. This is the heart of the affordability concern.
  • Surcharges can surprise customers.
  • Yearly true-ups are complex for the ICC and the public.
  • Some feel customers should benefit directly when they conserve.
  • Does not solve the cost of an aging pipe system.
Questions to ask

What guardrails, such as annual caps, will apply? How does it interact with the fixed fee assumption in the study? Does it apply to all customer classes?

D.1

Emissions Reduction Act

Say it this way

The Emissions Reduction Act is a voluntary plan. The utility files a multi-year investment plan, the ICC reviews it, and the costs are recovered through rates. It is offered as an alternative to a mandatory clean heat standard like Colorado's. Critics will ask how it is held accountable without a mandate.

In one sentence. A voluntary, utility-led capital plan for decarbonization investments, offered as an alternative to a mandatory clean heat standard.

Where it is used
  • Colorado has a clean heat standard. Xcel Energy must cut emissions 22 percent below 2015 levels by 2030, and its approved plan puts more than $440 million over three years mainly into electrification and efficiency.
  • Vermont passed a Clean Heat Standard in 2023. Fuel sellers must earn credits, and the rules have faced cost objections and an uncertain future.
  • Illinois has no mandatory clean heat standard today. The Emissions Reduction Act is the utility's alternative.
Who owns what

The utility would own the assets it builds, and customers would pay through rates once the ICC approves the plan. In a clean heat standard, obligated parties earn credits and may buy them from others.

Typical cost

Colorado's plan, at more than $440 million over three years for one utility, shows scale. A plan in Illinois would be sized and approved in a filing.

Time to build

Plan approval can take a year or more. In Colorado, regulators approved Xcel's plan after more than a year of discussion. Projects then run over multiple years.

Urban or rural fit

A plan can include any mix of projects, such as leak detection, hybrid programs, thermal networks and RNG, in cities and rural areas alike.

Pros
  • Flexible, since the utility picks the projects.
  • Avoids a one-size mandate.
  • Gives the ICC review before money is spent.
  • Can fund leak detection.
Cons
  • Voluntary plans lack a legal target, so critics say they may do too little.
  • A utility earns a return on capital, which can look like a built-in incentive to spend.
  • Ratepayers pay for it.
  • Without a deadline, progress can slip.
Questions to ask

What would the plan cost per customer per month? Who audits progress? How would it work alongside any legislation that sets a clean heat standard?

The six proposals side by side

ProposalWho pays firstWho owns the assetHow proven is itBiggest open question
Hybrid Heat PumpHomeowner, with a utility incentiveHomeownerCommon equipment, local program resultsWho pays the incentive
Thermal Energy NetworksUtility through approved rates, plus grantsUtility or a third partyA few U.S. pilots, the first commissioned in 2024Cost per customer at scale
Zonal Electrification TariffUtility and customers in the zoneCustomers own equipment, utility owns the gridPilot stageIs participation voluntary
RNG InterconnectionProducer today, utility incentive under the proposalProducer and utilityUsed elsewhere, with limited supplyReal supply and price
Revenue Balancing AdjustmentNone, it is a rate toolNot applicableAbout 18 states as of 2010, upheld in IllinoisAffordability guardrails
Emissions Reduction ActCustomers, after ICC approvalUtilityRelated models in Colorado and VermontAccountability without a mandate

Things that are easy to overlook

  • Fixed charges decide whether hybrids save money. RMI found high gas fixed charges limit savings, and the study assumes the fixed fee stays the same through 2050. Rate design may matter more than equipment.
  • A dual-fuel utility sits on both sides. A move from gas to electric is a shift between two systems of the same company, so cost allocation between gas and electric customers will draw scrutiny.
  • Gas storage and mains stand behind hybrid backup. Twelve storage fields and about 18,700 miles of mains are what a winter peak depends on.
  • Stranded costs. Every mile of main that stays carries cost that is spread over fewer customers if people leave. That is the logic of the zonal approach.
  • Contractors and workforce. A fast heat pump ramp needs trained installers, and gas workforce transition is part of the E3 metrics.
  • Legislation versus the ICC. The TEN bill HB 3609 stalled on the House floor and the CRGA created a pilot program instead.
  • Equity. Customers who cannot leave the gas system bear more of its cost as others exit, and consumer groups press on this.
  • Safety and leak detection. This works under any scenario, so it may be the easiest piece to defend publicly.
  • Customer data and consent. The pilot order says data sharing needs consent, which affects any hybrid or zonal pilot.

Knowledge center

Say it this way

A good first answer is short, says what the study does and does not do, and points to the ICC page for the official record. When you do not know a number, say it is in the E3 deck and you will confirm it.

35 common questions with plain answers. Search, filter by topic, or open them one at a time.

35 shown
01What is the Future of Gas proceeding?
Basics

It is an Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) docket, number 24-0158, that looks at what role natural gas utilities should play as Illinois pursues its climate goals. It grew out of the 2023 gas rate cases and runs in phases. The goal is a report to the Commission, due December 31, 2026, that lays out options rather than a final decision.

02Does the final report change anyone's rates or force a utility to do anything?
Basics

No, not by itself. The report informs the Commission, the legislature and stakeholders. Any change to rates, programs or obligations would need a separate order, a rate case, or a new law. Think of it as the map, not the road.

03Why is the ICC doing this?
Basics

Illinois law sets clean energy goals, and the gas system serves most homes for heating. Regulators want to understand what different paths would cost, how they affect reliability, and who pays. The 2023 gas rate cases raised the question of whether long-lived gas pipe investments still make sense, so the Commission opened a broader look.

04What do the phases mean?
Basics

Phase 1 gathered background and principles. Phase 2A and 2B ran pilots and pathways working groups. Phase 2C is the current phase, where the E3 Pathways Study results are in and utilities and other parties file proposals. After that comes the final report.

05Who takes part?
Basics

The ICC and its staff, the gas utilities including Ameren Illinois, consumer and environmental groups, labor, municipalities, industry groups and the consultant E3. Participation is mostly through workshops and written filings.

06What is the E3 Pathways Study?
The E3 study

It is a technical study by the consultant E3 that models how Illinois could reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 while still keeping homes and businesses heated. It tests several scenarios and compares them on cost, emissions, reliability and fairness.

07What does back-casting mean?
The E3 study

Instead of forecasting forward from today, the study starts from the goal, such as net zero by 2050 with a 35 percent cut by 2035, and works backward to see what would have to happen each decade. It shows what a path requires, not what will happen.

08What are the five scenarios?
The E3 study

They are High Electrification, High Geothermal, Hybrid Electrification, Hybrid Gas and Continued Gas Use. A business-as-usual baseline is included for comparison. They differ mainly in how many homes switch to electric heat, how many keep gas as a backup or primary fuel, and how much low-carbon fuel is assumed.

09How much do the scenarios cut emissions?
The E3 study

Per the E3 results deck, the emissions cuts are about 89, 89, 87, 78 and 78 percent for the five scenarios in the order above. The two electrification-heavy scenarios and the hybrid electrification scenario land close together, which is why the 87 versus 89 percent comparison is a key talking point.

10What do the scenarios cost?
The E3 study

The deck shows added cost in net present value of roughly $240, $220, $180, $180 and $240 billion for the five scenarios, in the same order. These are statewide, long-term totals, so they should not be read as a bill for any one household. Treat the figures as approximate and check the deck before quoting.

11Why is there still gas in 2050 in most scenarios?
The E3 study

Some uses are hard to electrify, such as certain industrial processes and the coldest peak days. The study shows about 200 trillion Btu of gas remaining in 2050, and it assumes large amounts of alternative fuels such as renewable natural gas and hydrogen in some scenarios. How realistic that supply is remains one of the biggest questions.

12What are the biggest uncertainties in the study?
The E3 study

The main ones are how fast people actually adopt heat pumps, how much renewable gas and hydrogen can really be produced, how much new electric generation and transmission can be built in time, and how carbon capture performs. The study is a set of what-if cases, so results move when those assumptions move.

13What is the IRP and how does it relate to this study?
Grid and the IRP

The Integrated Resource Plan is a separate state planning process required by the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA). The study's business-as-usual case matches the IRP base case, and its Hybrid Electrification case lines up with the IRP electrification case. That overlap is why the two timelines are being watched together.

14Why does electric peak demand matter so much?
Grid and the IRP

Winter heating on the coldest days is when gas does the heavy lifting today. If heating shifts to electricity, the grid must serve that load at the same moments. The deck shows electric peak growth of roughly 130, 94, 75, 54 and 48 percent across the scenarios, against 40 percent in business as usual.

15What is a hybrid or dual-fuel system?
Grid and the IRP

It pairs an electric heat pump with a gas furnace. The heat pump handles most of the year, and the furnace takes over on very cold days. In the E3 model the switchover happens at around 20 degrees Fahrenheit. The appeal is lower gas use with less strain on the grid at peak.

16What is a resource adequacy study?
Grid and the IRP

It checks whether there will be enough generation to keep the lights on in the future. The study released in January 2026 flagged possible risk in the MISO and PJM regions from about 2028 to 2031. It matters here because heavy electrification adds winter load on top of that.

17What does the ELCC term mean?
Grid and the IRP

Effective Load Carrying Capability. It measures how much a resource, such as a wind farm or battery, can be counted on during peak need, compared with a plant that is always available. Lower ELCC means more total capacity is needed to stay reliable.

18How does a heat pump work?
Technology

It moves heat rather than making it. In winter it pulls heat from outdoor air or the ground and delivers it inside. For each unit of electricity it can deliver roughly two to three units of heat, while a gas furnace delivers about 0.8 to 0.97. That ratio is called the coefficient of performance.

19How well do heat pumps work in Illinois winters?
Technology

Modern cold-climate models keep working at low temperatures, but efficiency and capacity drop as it gets colder. That is why many designs keep a backup, either electric resistance or a gas furnace. Real performance depends on the home, the installation and the equipment.

20What is a thermal energy network?
Technology

It is a shared loop of underground pipe carrying water at a mild temperature to many buildings, where each building's heat pump draws heat from the loop or returns heat to it. Framingham, Massachusetts, run by Eversource, is the best-known example, approved in 2020 and commissioned in June 2024. Illinois has a pilot funding path under CRGA of up to $20 million.

21What is a non-pipeline alternative?
Technology

A non-pipeline alternative, or NPA, is a way to meet customer needs without building or replacing gas pipe, for example by electrifying a block or adding efficiency. Whether and how utilities must evaluate NPAs is being handled in legislative or follow-up proceedings rather than in this docket.

22What is renewable natural gas?
Technology

RNG is pipeline-quality gas made from sources such as landfills, farms or wastewater. It can be blended into the existing system, but supply is limited and cost varies a lot. A key policy question is who pays to connect RNG producers to the system and how much revenue a connection must be expected to produce.

23What is a clean heat standard?
Technology

It is a rule that requires fuel suppliers or utilities to deliver a rising share of clean heat, often through credits for heat pumps and efficiency. Colorado and Vermont have versions. It is different from Illinois' voluntary approach, where programs are offered but not required.

24What has Ameren Illinois proposed in Phase 2C?
Ameren Illinois proposals

Six proposals. They cover hybrid heat pump incentives (C.2), a thermal energy network pilot (G.1), a zonal electrification approach (C.1), renewable natural gas interconnection (A.1), a revenue balancing adjustment (F.6) and an emissions reduction approach (D.1). The page and guide explain each in plain language.

25What is the hybrid heat pump program?
Ameren Illinois proposals

Incentives and rebates that help customers pair a heat pump with an existing gas furnace. It supports lower gas use while protecting winter reliability. It is the proposal most directly supported by the study's hybrid scenarios.

26What is zonal electrification?
Ameren Illinois proposals

It targets specific neighborhoods or zones where gas pipe is aging and electrifying customers together could be cheaper than replacing the pipe. A four-site zonal study is underway, with a report due December 31 for use in the next rate case.

27What is a revenue balancing adjustment?
Ameren Illinois proposals

It is a rate mechanism that adjusts what the utility collects so that revenue does not rise or fall just because customers use less gas. Supporters say it removes the utility's incentive to discourage efficiency. Critics worry it shifts risk to customers. The Illinois Supreme Court has upheld a gas volume balancing rider, though Ameren's current gas rider should be confirmed.

28Why does a gas utility propose programs that reduce gas use?
Ameren Illinois proposals

State goals, customer demand for efficiency, and the risk of stranded pipe costs all push in that direction. Programs such as hybrids and zonal pilots let the utility shape the transition and keep customers served, rather than waiting for others to set the terms.

29Where do the proposals stand now?
Ameren Illinois proposals

They were filed in Phase 2C and are being discussed in workshops. Parties can respond through workshops and written filings, and the Commission's final report will reflect the discussion. Nothing in them is final.

30Will the study make my gas or electric bill go up?
Costs and bills

The study does not set bills. It compares long-term system costs under different paths. Household effects depend on the equipment, the home, rates and incentives. The deck's appendix illustrates monthly Ameren bills in 2050, for example about $203 for an efficient furnace and about $246 for all-electric, which are scenario illustrations rather than forecasts.

31What does it cost a homeowner to install a heat pump?
Costs and bills

Costs vary widely with home size, ductwork, electrical upgrades and region, and published ranges run from a few thousand dollars to well over ten thousand. Use outside figures only as rough benchmarks. Ameren Illinois' own program costs depend on the filed proposals and are not estimated here.

32Who ultimately pays for a transition?
Costs and bills

It depends on the design. Costs can fall on participants, on all ratepayers through riders, on taxpayers through grants and incentives, or on shareholders. Much of the policy debate is about how to split these fairly, especially for lower-income customers who cannot easily switch.

33What are the key dates to remember?
Process and dates

The final Future of Gas report is due December 31, 2026. The IRP has a mid-November timeline, and the zonal electrification study reports by December 31. Always confirm dates on the ICC site, since schedules shift.

34How can the public take part?
Process and dates

By attending workshops, reading the posted presentations on the ICC Future of Gas pages, and filing comments in the docket. Stakeholders may also respond to the Phase 2C proposals through the process the ICC sets out.

35Where do I find the official materials?
Process and dates

On the ICC Future of Gas pages, which list workshop presentations, the schedule, the topics and the Pilot 2C materials, and in the e-docket for 24-0158. This guide is a learning aid and not a substitute for those sources.
